newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Chronology - Ten days that shook Papua New Guinea.
newsitem.headline: Chronology - Ten days that shook Papua New Guinea.

text.p: The most serious political crisis in Papua New Guinea's 22 years as an independent nation was sparked by its most intractable problem, a nine-year independence battle on the resource-rich island of Bougainville.
Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan hired foreign mercenaries to help win the war, part of a plan which he said included buying and reopening Bougainville's long-closed Panguna copper mine.
But the multi-million dollar contract with British-based Sandline was taken as a direct affront by the underpaid and ill-equipped Papua New Guinea defence force:

March 17 - Defence force commander Brigadier General Jerry Singirok gives Chan a 48-hour deadline to quit over his decision to hire the mercenaries, alleging corruption. "I want to state clearly that we do not have a coup," states Singarok, who says he remains committed to democracy. Chan calls late night cabinet meeting which sacks Singirok as defence force head.
March 18 - Chan asserts he is in "absolute control". Singirok agrees to step down and urges calm. Australia and New Zealand support elected government. Crisis appears to ease.

March 19 - Anti-government protest erupts in violence as thousands of demonstrators clash with police and loot shops. A senior army officer backs Singirok, but troops stay in barracks. Six mercenaries fly out, and about 50 others are detained by the army. Chan hints mercenaries may not be used on Bougainville.

March 20 - Crisis deepens as protestors and army demand reinstatement of Singirok. Police fire teargas and shots ring out through capital as thousands protest. Chan says Sandline contract is suspended and will be investigated by a commission of inquiry.

March 21 - Singirok releases Sandline contract showing mercenaries hired as frontline troops, not just advisors. Dozens of Sandline personnel head home. Singirok issues Tuesday deadline for Chan and two senior ministers to quit.

March 22 - Rebel army officers supporting Singirok say they are in control of the army. Some 48 mercenaries arrive in Johannesburg. Sandline chief, former British colonel Tim Spicer, still in Port Moresby. Australian troops put on standby to evacuate nationals if crisis worsens.

March 23 - Chan addresses nation on televsion. "I am not going to resign," he says. Respected former prime minister Sir Michael Somare says mercenary plan was "stupid". Opposition says it will move motion in parliament requesting Chan's resignation.

March 24 - Sandline's Spicer pleads not guilty to possessing unlicensed pistol and ammunition and is bailed to stand trial on April 8. Four ministers in Chan's cabinet resign. Effective head of state Sir Wiwa Korowi urges Chan to step down.

March 25 - Chan survives motion in parliament urging his resignation by 58 votes to 39 after five hours of rowdy debate. About 80 heavily armed soldiers and thousands of protestors besiege parliament overnight, stopping politicians leaving.

March 26 - Chan gives in to mounting pressure and says he will step aside to defuse the crisis. Chan says he will ask cabinet to nominate a caretaker administration ahead of national elections, due in June.
